description: Hey, we are 3 students from NUST interested in delivering a project which reflects our passion for space and making the exploration of its magical vastness accessible for everyone around.
summary:
What if you could hear the Earth changing, even without seeing it?

Every day, satellites capture incredible stories about our planet: temperatures rising, oceans moving, forests changing, lightning striking and cities illuminating the night. But what if these stories could be experienced through sound?

Introducing AURA – Audible Understanding of Remote-sensing & Atmospheric Data, developed by The Orion's Belt.

AURA transforms Earth observation information into soundscapes, offering a new way to explore our planet beyond traditional maps and graphs. Using NASA Earth science resources, data processing, machine learning and audio synthesis, the platform translates environmental patterns into changes in pitch, rhythm and intensity.

From the pulse of global temperatures to the rhythm of lightning, AURA makes complex Earth science more engaging and opens another sensory pathway for people with visual impairments.

Our mission is to make the science of our planet accessible, intuitive and immersive.

Because understanding Earth shouldn't depend on sight alone.
details:
A New Way to Experience Our Planet

Imagine exploring the movement of ocean currents without looking at a map, or experiencing changes in global temperatures through sound. Imagine satellite observations becoming something you can not only explore, but listen to.

That is the idea behind AURA.

Developed by The Orion's Belt, AURA is an interactive, accessibility-focused platform that transforms Earth observation information into auditory experiences. It explores how sound can make complex scientific information easier to experience, understand and communicate.

What does AURA do?

AURA brings together seven Earth science experiences, each inspired by a different aspect of our changing planet:

  • Earth at Night: Discover how nighttime illumination changes across our planet, revealing patterns of human activity and urban development.
  • Ocean Pulse: Explore the movement of ocean currents and variations in sea surface temperature.
  • Atmospheric Breath: Discover the movement of atmospheric aerosols, including dust and other airborne particles.

Not just this, our project includes data of global sea surface currents and temperature, air quality, Earth lightning as well as carbondioxide concentrations. Each experience brings together a relevant NASA visualization, an auditory representation and an explanation to help users understand what they are exploring.

AURA also features a separate Image-to-Sound Studio, where users can upload their own images or videos and experiment with transforming visual features into sound.

How does it work?

At its heart, AURA follows a simple idea: scientific information can be represented through more than numbers and pictures.

The platform uses three interconnected stages:

1. Discover – Bringing Earth observations to life

AURA draws inspiration from NASA Earth science resources and scientific visualizations. Relevant information is retrieved and prepared for exploration, allowing users to engage with different environmental phenomena through dedicated experiences.

2. Understand – Finding patterns in the data

Data processing and machine learning help identify patterns, variations and unusual observations.

For example, our Temperature Pulse experience uses NASA GISTEMP temperature records and an Isolation Forest model to identify statistically unusual patterns in rolling temperature observations. Rather than treating every unusual observation as a climate event, the system uses anomaly detection to highlight patterns worth exploring.

3. Listen – Turning information into sound

The sonification engine translates selected data characteristics into auditory properties such as pitch, rhythm, intensity and harmonic variation.

For instance, temperature anomalies can influence pitch, while changes between observations can influence the harmonic character of the sound. This creates an auditory representation that allows listeners to experience variations that might otherwise be difficult to notice in a table of numbers.

The Image-to-Sound Studio follows a complementary approach, extracting visual features such as brightness and contrast from uploaded images or videos and mapping them into sound.

What makes AURA different?

Most Earth observation platforms communicate through maps, graphs and satellite imagery. While powerful, these approaches depend heavily on visual interpretation.

AURA asks a different question:

What if satellite data could tell its story through sound?

Instead of simply attaching music to scientific images, AURA explores meaningful mappings between environmental information and auditory characteristics. A changing temperature pattern, a burst of lightning activity or a shift in ocean conditions can each inspire a distinct soundscape.

This makes AURA more than an audio player. It is an exploration of sonification as a tool for science communication, accessibility and learning.

Who can benefit?

Our intended audience includes:

  • People with visual impairments: An additional sensory pathway for engaging with Earth science, complementing accessible text and other assistive technologies.
  • Students and educators: A creative approach to understanding environmental phenomena and making abstract scientific concepts more memorable.
  • Science enthusiasts: An interactive way to explore NASA Earth science resources beyond conventional visualizations.
  • The wider public: An opportunity to connect with environmental changes through an engaging, multisensory experience.

Our long-term vision is to make scientific information more inclusive and to encourage people to connect with the planet through curiosity and discovery.

Technology and tools

AURA was developed using a combination of open-source technologies and scientific resources:

  • Python: Core application development, data processing and audio generation.
  • Streamlit: Interactive web application and user interface.
  • Pandas and NumPy: Data manipulation and numerical operations.
  • Scikit-learn: Machine learning, including Isolation Forest anomaly detection and exploratory clustering.
  • SciPy: Numerical and audio signal processing.
  • OpenCV: Image and video feature extraction.
  • NASA Scientific Visualization Studio: Earth science visualizations and supporting scientific resources.
  • Text-to-speech tools: Supporting spoken explanations and auditory accessibility.

Design considerations and future impact

Throughout development, we considered scientific accuracy, accessibility, usability and interpretability. An important design principle was distinguishing actual scientific measurements from features extracted from rendered images. A visual pattern should never be presented as a calibrated physical measurement unless it is supported by the underlying scientific data.

We also aimed to make the platform approachable for people without a technical background, while retaining enough scientific context to make the experience meaningful.

AURA is a step towards a more inclusive way of communicating science. By introducing sound as another way to explore Earth observations, we hope to make environmental knowledge accessible to audiences who are often left out of traditionally visual experiences.

We can see the Earth through satellites. With AURA, we want to help everyone hear its story.
